{"id":"PKIX-0lbp","title":"diff-harness CRL adapter lacks signer discovery and cRLIssuer support: ~18 PKITS vectors","description":"## What the 20 chains actually need

Checked one by one, building the adapter's checkers and recording every outcome per certificate. My earlier claim that all 20 were the reason-partitioned CRL gap was wrong: only TWO are.

  cause                                                  chains  fix belongs in
  CrlSignatureInvalid -- CRL signed by a different key       ~9  THE ADAPTER
    of the same CA (key rollover / separate CRL key)
  CrlIssuerMismatch -- indirect CRL via cRLIssuer            ~7  THE ADAPTER
  OutOfScope -- onlySomeReasons reason partitioning            2  the library
  no undetermined cert in my probe (4.5.4, 4.5.6)             2  probe artifact

## Group A: CRL signed by a different key of the same CA (~9 chains)

4.11.7, 4.12.7, 4.12.9, 4.13.19, 4.5.1, 4.6.15, 4.6.17, 4.9.6, 4.4.19

Every one reports CrlSignatureInvalid for at least one checker. PKITS classes them valid, so the CRL IS validly signed -- just not by the certificate the adapter passes as the issuer. These are the self-issued key-rollover and "Separate Certificate and CRL Keys" vectors: the CA holds several certificates and the CRL is signed by one of them while the certificate under test was signed by another. The adapter always passes chain[i+1], which is the signature-chain issuer, not necessarily the CRL signer.

pkix-revocation already solves this. CrlChecker::new_with_signer_discovery(crl_der, bundle, cert_to_check, now, verifier) takes a bundle of candidate signers and discovers which one signed the CRL. Its own documentation says it is "the right choice when the bundle is already known to be path-valid (e.g. pkix-chain already validated it)" -- which is exactly the harness's position, since it validates the path before checking revocation.

The adapter never calls it. PKITS CertPath carries the extra CA certificates; they are available and unused.

## Group B: indirect CRLs (~7 chains)

4.14.22, 4.14.24, 4.14.25, 4.14.28, 4.14.29, 4.14.30, 4.14.33

All report CrlIssuerMismatch. These are the indirectCRL and cRLIssuer vectors, where the CRL is issued by an entity other than the certificate's issuer.

pkix-revocation solves this too, via new_with_crl_issuer and with_delta_and_crl_issuer. The adapter calls neither.

Probing every CertPath certificate as a candidate cRLIssuer resolved three outright:

  4.14.22  indirectCRLCA1CRL.crl       with issuer = cert[1]
  4.14.30  indirectCRLCA4cRLIssuerCRL  with issuer = cert[2]
  4.14.33  indirectCRLCA5CRL.crl       with issuer = cert[1]

The other four did not resolve with a naive sweep. That does NOT mean they cannot: my probe held chain[i+1] as the issuer argument while varying only the cRLIssuer, and for an indirect CRL both may need to differ. Not established either way.

## Group C: the real library gap (2 chains)

4.14.18, 4.14.19 -- Valid onlySomeReasons Test18 and Test19. Both report OutOfScope.

This is the limitation a407f615 documented when it introduced it: "Combining reason-partitioned CRLs is not implemented, so valid vectors such as PKITS 4.14.18 are now out of scope rather than passed." Determining status needs several reason-partitioned CRLs combined, which pkix-revocation does not do.

Two PKITS vectors, not twenty. Still a genuine missing feature, and now correctly sized.

## Two chains I could not classify

4.5.4 and 4.5.6 produced no undetermined certificate in my probe, so my reconstruction of the chain differs from the harness's. The harness reorders PKITS CertPath bundles with pkix-path-builder because several §4.4, §4.5 and §4.14 vectors advertise CRL-signing certificates that are not in the signature chain. My probe just reversed CertPath and dropped the anchor.

That difference is itself a hint: those two likely involve exactly the extra CRL-signing certificate that path building moves, which is Group A's shape.

## What this means

Eighteen of twenty are adapter gaps of the same class as the delta-CRL pairing just fixed: the library has the capability, the harness does not use it. The pattern has now repeated three times -- single CRLs instead of base+delta, signature-chain issuer instead of discovered CRL signer, no cRLIssuer support -- so the adapter's CRL handling is simply much thinner than pkix-revocation's.

## Acceptance

[ ] Adapter uses new_with_signer_discovery with the full CertPath bundle, so a CRL signed by another of the CA's keys is found
[ ] Adapter tries cRLIssuer constructions for indirect CRLs, including with_delta_and_crl_issuer
[ ] Re-run and recount: Group A and B should mostly clear
[ ] Classify 4.5.4 and 4.5.6 against the harness's own reordered chain rather than a hand-rolled one
[ ] Decide reason-partitioned CRL combining on its real size: 2 vectors","status":"open","priority":2,"issue_type":"bug","owner":"mark@reviewcommit.com","created_at":"2026-11-25T03:23:06.6308854Z","created_by":"Mark Atwood","updated_at":"2026-11-25T03:23:06.6308854Z"}

{"notes":"ATTEMPTED AND REVERTED 2026-11-25. The brute-force approach clears 18 of 20 target chains and breaks 18 negative tests doing it. Net zero, in the dangerous direction. Reverted; the design needs to change, not the effort.

## What I built

- Chain gained aux_certs_der, carrying the certificates path building drops. Needed because try_build_chain returns only the built path plus the anchor, so a CA's CRL-signing certificate -- a sibling of the chain, not a link in it -- never reached the oracle at all.
- build_checkers offered every bundle certificate as a cRLIssuer candidate, via new_with_crl_issuer and with_delta_and_crl_issuer.
- discovery_checkers called new_with_signer_discovery per certificate with the whole bundle.

## It worked on the targets

18 of the 20 cleared. Only 4.14.18 and 4.14.19 remained, which are the genuine onlySomeReasons library gap.

## And broke 18 negative tests

  4.4.1   Missing CRL Test1                           no CRL at all
  4.4.4   Invalid Bad CRL Signature Test4             CRL signature is bad
  4.4.5   Invalid Bad CRL Issuer Name Test5           CRL issuer name is wrong
  4.4.6   Invalid Wrong CRL Test6                     wrong CRL entirely
  4.4.8   Invalid Unknown CRL Entry Extension Test8   (previously fixed, re-broken)
  4.4.9   Invalid Unknown CRL Extension Test9         (previously fixed, re-broken)
  4.4.10  Invalid Unknown CRL Extension Test10
  4.4.11  Invalid Old CRL nextUpdate Test11
  4.4.12  Invalid pre2000 CRL nextUpdate Test12
  4.4.21  Invalid Separate Certificate and CRL Keys Test21
  4.7.4   Invalid keyUsage Critical cRLSign False     signer lacks cRLSign
  4.7.5   Invalid keyUsage Not Critical cRLSign False signer lacks cRLSign
  4.14.9  Invalid distributionPoint Test9
  4.14.11 Invalid onlyContainsUserCerts CRL Test11
  4.14.12 Invalid onlyContainsCACerts CRL Test12
  4.14.14 Invalid onlyContainsAttributeCerts Test14
  4.14.17 Invalid onlySomeReasons Test17
  4.15.1  Invalid deltaCRLIndicator No Base Test1

  class              baseline  paired   with sweep
  LooserThanWild           81      43           77
  StricterThanWild         46      77           43
  gt disagreements         46      35           35

Net ground-truth agreement did not move. The composition traded 18 valid-chain fixes for 18 invalid-chain regressions, and LooserThanWild -- accepting what others reject -- went back up from 43 to 77.

## Where my reasoning was wrong, precisely

I justified candidate sweeping by analogy to the delta pairing: "offering candidates is safe because the library enforces the real rules." That held for with_delta, which enforces a specific base-to-delta relationship and rejects a pairing that does not belong.

It does NOT hold for cRLIssuer and signer sweeping, because the sweep changes the question being asked. Instead of

  "is this CRL usable for this certificate, per the certificate's own
   distribution point?"

it asks

  "does there exist ANY certificate in the bundle that makes SOME CRL
   usable for this certificate?"

Several of the broken tests exist precisely because no valid relationship exists -- a bad signature, a wrong issuer name, the wrong CRL, a signer without cRLSign. Searching hard enough until something validates is the definition of defeating them.

The analogy failed on a property I did not check: whether the library's validation is sufficient to reject a wrong candidate, or merely necessary.

## What a correct implementation looks like

Follow RFC 5280 §6.3.3 rather than enumerating. Read the certificate's own CRLDistributionPoints, use the DP to select which CRL applies and which cRLIssuer is named, and check that one. Candidate selection becomes DP-driven rather than exhaustive, so a certificate with no matching DP stays undetermined instead of being matched by brute force.

That also needs the keyUsage check on the discovered signer: 4.7.4 and 4.7.5 turn on cRLSign being absent, and whether new_with_signer_discovery enforces that is an open question worth answering before relying on it.

aux_certs_der is still required by any correct version, since those CRL-signing certificates genuinely are dropped before the oracle sees them. It was reverted along with everything else rather than left as a breaking public field change serving no working code -- three test files construct Chain literally.

## Acceptance

[ ] Answer: does new_with_signer_discovery check the discovered signer's keyUsage cRLSign bit?
[ ] Re-implement DP-driven: read CRLDistributionPoints, select CRL and cRLIssuer from it, no enumeration
[ ] Re-add aux_certs_der when there is working code that needs it, fixing the Chain literals in the three test files
[ ] Target: clear the 18 WITHOUT regressing the 18 negative tests. Both counts must be checked, which this attempt proves is not optional","title":"diff-harness CRL adapter: DP-driven signer and cRLIssuer selection (brute force rejected)"}

{"notes":"THREE STRATEGIES MEASURED, ALL WORSE THAN DOING NOTHING. Reverted. The search space is now mapped; the shortcut does not exist.

## Measured

  strategy                                            gt disagreements   LooserThanWild
  (committed baseline, no change)                                   35               43
  1. enumerate cRLIssuer candidates + signer discovery              35               77
  2. signer discovery only, whole bundle                            44               74
  3. signer discovery, candidates restricted to certs whose
     subject DN equals the CRL's issuer DN                          46               76

Strategy 1 was a net-zero trade: it cleared 18 of the 20 target chains and broke 18 negative tests doing it. Strategies 2 and 3 were worse outright.

## Why each failed, which is the useful part

STRATEGY 1 -- enumeration. Offering every bundle certificate as a cRLIssuer asks "does there exist any certificate that makes some CRL usable" instead of "is this CRL usable for this certificate per its distribution point". Vectors like Invalid Bad CRL Signature, Invalid Wrong CRL and Invalid keyUsage cRLSign False exist precisely because no valid relationship exists, so searching until something validates defeats them by construction.

Specifically relevant: new_with_crl_issuer OMITS the cRLSign KeyUsage check for a trust anchor -- crl.rs says so, "anchors are trusted by construction; they carry no KeyUsage to inspect" -- and the sweep offered the anchor as a candidate. That is how 4.7.4 and 4.7.5 broke.

STRATEGY 2 -- signer discovery alone. I expected this to be the safe half, because new_with_signer_discovery is self-validating: it runs check_crl_sign for RFC 5280 §6.3.3(f) and requires reaches_self_signed. Both hold, and it still regressed 9 chains.

The reason is that discover_crl_signer(bundle, &crl) searches the bundle for whoever signed the CRL. That answers "who signed this" when the question is "is this the right CRL for this certificate". Invalid Wrong CRL presents a CRL that IS validly signed by a bundle member, so discovery finds the signer, cRLSign passes, chain-up passes, and the wrong CRL is accepted.

STRATEGY 3 -- restrict discovery to certificates whose subject DN equals the CRL's issuer DN, which is exactly the key-rollover shape: one CA, several certificates, same subject, different keys. Reasoned from the mechanism rather than guessed, and still worse: 46, the same as the original stale baseline.

## What this establishes

Every candidate-set strategy fails the same way. The adapter's defect is not which candidates it considers -- it is that it asks whether ANY (certificate, CRL) pairing validates, while RFC 5280 §6.3.3 specifies a SELECTION: for each certificate the distribution point determines which CRL and which issuer, and exactly that pairing is checked.

Negative tests are built so that no valid pairing exists while some invalid pairing superficially validates. Enumeration cannot distinguish those. No amount of narrowing the candidate set fixes a procedure that is structurally the wrong question.

## What a correct implementation requires

Implement §6.3.3 selection rather than search:

1. Read the certificate's CRLDistributionPoints extension.
2. For each DP: take its distributionPoint name and its cRLIssuer field.
3. Select the CRL whose own IssuingDistributionPoint and issuer match that DP. Do not consider any other CRL for this certificate.
4. Construct one checker for that pairing -- new_with_crl_issuer when the DP names a cRLIssuer, otherwise the plain or delta-paired form.
5. A certificate with no matching DP stays undetermined. That is the point: it must not be rescued by a CRL it never pointed at.

Note this partly duplicates matching pkix-revocation already performs internally -- OutOfScope(CrlDistributionPointIssuerMismatch) comes from there. Worth checking first whether the library can expose the selection rather than the harness restating it, because a second DP-matching implementation is the same divergence hazard that kept wildcard matching in one place.

## Honest status

Not fixed. Three attempts, each measured against ground truth and each reverted. What is delivered is a mapped search space: the three obvious strategies are recorded as worse than doing nothing, with the mechanism for each, so the next attempt starts from selection rather than rediscovering that search fails.

The committed baseline and the gate are untouched and green.

## Acceptance

[x] Answered: new_with_signer_discovery DOES check cRLSign (§6.3.3(f)) and requires reaches_self_signed; new_with_crl_issuer omits the cRLSign check for trust anchors
[x] Enumeration strategies measured and rejected with reasons
[ ] Check whether pkix-revocation can expose §6.3.3 DP selection, so the harness does not restate it
[ ] Implement DP-driven selection per the five steps above
[ ] Target: clear the 18 adapter-gap chains WITHOUT regressing the 18 negative tests. Both counts, every time -- all three failed attempts looked fine on one of them"}
